"I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq," Gates said. "I also did not want Gen. Petraeus hanging out there all by himself. "While the analyses of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, CentCom and Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president's senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus," he said. "Extremist Islam was dramatically empowered by defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The first attack against us by the extremists, the World Trade Center in 1993, was launched from Afghanistan just four years after the last Soviet soldier left there. "Should the jihadists be able to claim a victory in Iraq over the United States, the sole remaining superpower, I believe it would empower them worldwide far, far more than their victory over the Soviets," Gates said. outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- If he had known then what he knows now, he might have made different decisions before the start of the Iraq war in 2003, the outgoing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff told reporters Friday.

Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace said he now believes more troops were needed at the outset of the war.

“One of the mistakes I made in my assumptions going in was that the Iraqi people and the Iraqi Army would welcome liberation, that the Iraqi Army, given the opportunity, would stand together for the Iraqi people and be available to them to help serve the new nation,” Pace said.

Instead, “they disintegrated in the face of the coalition’s first several weeks of combat, so they weren’t here,” he said.

Had he known that would happen, Pace said, he would have recommended sending more troops at the beginning of the Iraq war.

Pace also said that, had he been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should increase its Army and Marine Corps contingents in Iraq, he would have said no, because the plan at the time was to build and equip an Iraqi Army and transfer security responsibilities to it.

The force was built and equipped, Pace said, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque — one of the holiest Shiite sites — inflamed long-standing tensions between Sunni and Shiite Muslims, further destabilizing the region and derailing any plans to reduce U.S. troop levels. Thousands of people have died in reprisal killings and bombings since the attack.

Still, Pace said, “Given what I knew at the time, I’m comfortable with the recommendations that I made.”

Any errors that were made should be learned from, he added.

He also continued to express support for the Iraq invasion.

“Twenty-six million Iraqis have the opportunity now,” he said. “They are working their way through 3½ decades of being trod upon, held down, no opportunity at all for freedom of expression, for living their lives the way they wanted to, for picking [their] leaders.”

Pace is set to retire when his two-year term ends this month.

Also Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates — in his first public comments since President Bush announced Thursday night that he was accepting Gen. David Petraeus’ recommendation on Iraq troop levels — noted that all of Bush’s senior military advisers agreed with those recommendations.

Gates said he had asked Pace and Adm. William Fallon, the head of U.S. Central Command, to begin examining U.S. options in Iraq months earlier, knowing that Petraeus — the top U.S. commander in Iraq — was conducting a similar review.

“I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq,” Gates said. “I also did not want Gen. Petraeus hanging out there all by himself.

“While the analyses of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, CentCom and Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president’s senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus,” he said.

The United States’ next steps in Iraq, among other considerations, “had to avoid even the appearance of American failure,” Gates said.

“Extremist Islam was dramatically empowered by defeating the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The first attack against us by the extremists, the World Trade Center in 1993, was launched from Afghanistan just four years after the last Soviet soldier left there.

“Should the jihadists be able to claim a victory in Iraq over the United States, the sole remaining superpower, I believe it would empower them worldwide far, far more than their victory over the Soviets,” Gates said. “The regional consequences would be significant and highly destabilizing.”
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Gen. Peter Pace, the outgoing chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told reporters Friday that, with the benefit of hindsight, he might have advised differently before the Iraq war began in 2003.

Pace said he now believes a larger number of U.S. troops should have been deployed at the beginning of the conflict. He explained that one of his incorrect assumptions was that Iraqis, including the Iraqi Army, would embrace liberation and that Iraqi forces would remain unified and help support the country’s new government.

Instead, he said, the Iraqi Army collapsed during the coalition’s first several weeks of fighting and was no longer available to help stabilize the country. If he had known that would happen, Pace said, he would have recommended sending more troops from the start.

Pace also said that, had he been asked in January 2006 whether the United States should increase the size of its Army and Marine Corps presence in Iraq, he would have opposed doing so. At that point, he said, the strategy was to create, train and equip an Iraqi Army, then hand over security responsibilities to those forces.

According to Pace, that Iraqi force was established and supplied, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque, one of Shiite Islam’s most sacred sites, inflamed longstanding Sunni-Shiite tensions. The attack further destabilized Iraq and ended hopes for reducing U.S. troop levels at that time. Since the bombing, thousands have been killed in retaliatory violence and bomb attacks.

Even so, Pace said he remains at ease with the advice he gave based on what he understood then. He added that any mistakes should be studied and used as lessons.

Pace also continued to defend the decision to invade Iraq. He said 26 million Iraqis now have an opportunity after 35 years of oppression, during which they lacked freedom of expression, the ability to live as they chose and the right to select their leaders.

Pace is set to retire when his two-year term concludes later this month.

Also on Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates made his first public remarks since President Bush announced Thursday night that he would accept Gen. David Petraeus’ recommendation on troop levels in Iraq. Gates emphasized that all of Bush’s top military advisers supported Petraeus’ recommendations.

Gates said he had asked Pace and Adm. William Fallon, commander of U.S. Central Command, months earlier to begin reviewing possible U.S. courses of action in Iraq, while knowing that Petraeus, the top American commander in Iraq, was conducting his own assessment.

Gates said he wanted the president to hear from more than one senior military leader while deciding the next steps in Iraq. He also said he did not want Petraeus left alone as the only public military voice behind the recommendations.

Although the analyses from the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Central Command and Petraeus differed in focus and method, Gates said all of the president’s senior military advisers fully agreed with Petraeus’ proposals.

Gates also said U.S. policy in Iraq needed, among other goals, to avoid even the perception of an American defeat. He argued that extremist Islam gained major strength after the Soviet Union was driven out of Afghanistan. Gates noted that the first extremist attack against the United States, the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, was launched from Afghanistan only four years after the final Soviet soldier departed.

If jihadists were able to portray Iraq as a victory over the United States, Gates said, it would strengthen them globally far more than their defeat of the Soviets did. He warned that the regional effects would be serious and deeply destabilizing.

Gen. Peter Pace said he would have recommended sending more U.S. troops at the start of the Iraq war if he had known that the Iraqi Army would collapse as quickly as it did. Looking back, Pace said one of his key assumptions had been wrong: he believed that both the Iraqi people and the Iraqi Army would welcome liberation from Saddam Hussein’s regime and would help the United States build a new Iraqi nation.

Pace also said that, despite later criticism of troop levels, he would not have supported a major U.S. troop buildup in January 2006. At that time, he said, the U.S. strategy was focused on transferring security responsibilities to a newly created Iraqi Army. The goal was to strengthen Iraqi forces so they could take over more duties and allow American troops eventually to reduce their role.

However, events soon changed the situation on the ground. The bombing of the Golden Mosque in February 2006 sharply escalated sectarian violence between Sunnis and Shiites. That increase in violence disrupted U.S. plans to reduce troop levels and complicated efforts to hand over security responsibilities to Iraqi forces.

Even so, Pace said he remained comfortable with the recommendations he made based on the information available to him at the time. He also said he continued to support the original decision to invade Iraq.

Outgoing Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Peter Pace said that, in hindsight, he would have recommended sending more U.S. troops into Iraq at the start of the 2003 invasion if he had known that the Iraqi Army would collapse instead of remaining available to help stabilize the country.

Reflecting on the assumptions that shaped the early stages of the war, Pace said U.S. planners believed Iraqi military units could be used after the fall of Saddam Hussein to help provide security, maintain order, and support the transition to a new government. That expectation proved wrong when the Iraqi Army disintegrated, leaving coalition forces with far fewer local security partners than anticipated.

Pace said that if he had known then what later became clear, he would have advised a larger initial American force. More troops, he suggested, might have been needed to secure the country, protect key infrastructure, and prevent the disorder that followed the fall of Baghdad.

He also addressed the later failure of U.S. plans to transfer security responsibilities to Iraqi forces as quickly as officials had hoped. Pace said those plans were disrupted by the rise of sectarian violence, which intensified after the invasion and made it much harder for Iraqi police and military units to take control of their own security. The violence between Sunni and Shiite groups, along with insurgent attacks and militia activity, forced the United States to reassess its strategy and remain more deeply involved than expected.

Despite those setbacks, Pace defended the decisions made by military leaders at the time. He argued that commanders and policymakers acted on the best information available to them, even though some of the key assumptions later proved inaccurate. He said it was unfair to judge every decision solely by what became known afterward.

Pace also maintained that the invasion removed a brutal dictator and gave Iraqis an opportunity to build a freer society. While acknowledging the heavy costs of the war and the difficulties that followed, he said the effort had given the Iraqi people a chance to determine their own future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Gen. Peter Pace admitting that more troops should have been sent at the start of the Iraq War, including his comments on Iraqi forces, the Golden Mosque bombing, and Robert Gates’ support for Petraeus’ troop recommendations.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pace: U.S. should have sent more troops at start of Iraq War**

WASHINGTON — Gen. Peter Pace, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, acknowledged that the United States should have deployed more troops at the beginning of the Iraq War, saying a larger force may have helped contain the violence and instability that followed the 2003 invasion.

Pace said U.S. commanders and policymakers underestimated the number of troops needed to secure Iraq after the fall of Saddam Hussein’s government. His comments amounted to one of the clearest admissions from a senior military leader that the initial U.S. force was too small to maintain order in the country.

The general said the early troop levels were not sufficient to deal with the widespread looting, the collapse of Iraqi institutions and the emergence of armed groups that later fueled the insurgency.

Pace also addressed the performance of Iraqi security forces, saying they had improved but still faced serious challenges. He said Iraqi units were increasingly taking part in operations alongside U.S. troops, but many still depended on American forces for logistics, intelligence, transportation and firepower.

The goal, Pace said, remained to build Iraqi forces capable of securing the country on their own, but he indicated that progress varied widely from unit to unit and region to region.

Pace pointed to the February 2006 bombing of the Golden Mosque in Samarra as a major turning point in the conflict. The attack on one of Shiite Islam’s holiest shrines triggered a wave of sectarian killings and retaliatory violence between Sunni and Shiite groups, sharply worsening Iraq’s security crisis.

The bombing, Pace said, changed the nature of the war by accelerating sectarian conflict and placing additional pressure on both U.S. and Iraqi forces.

His remarks came as Defense Secretary Robert Gates expressed support for Gen. David Petraeus, the top U.S. commander in Iraq, and his recommendations on troop levels. Gates said Petraeus’ judgment would carry significant weight in decisions about how many American forces should remain in Iraq and for how long.

Petraeus had overseen the troop increase known as the “surge,” which sent additional U.S. forces into Iraq in an effort to reduce violence, particularly in Baghdad and surrounding areas. Gates said decisions on future withdrawals would depend on conditions on the ground and the advice of commanders.

The comments underscored the continuing debate in Washington over whether the United States entered Iraq with too few troops, whether Iraqi forces were ready to assume responsibility for security, and how quickly American forces could be reduced without risking further instability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a 2007 CNN report from Washington on outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace reflecting on mistakes made in Iraq, with quotes from Pace and Defense Secretary Robert Gates.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Outgoing Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Peter Pace said Thursday the United States made “significant mistakes” in Iraq, but he defended the commitment of American troops and said military leaders have an obligation to learn from what went wrong.

Speaking as he prepared to leave the Pentagon’s top uniformed post, Pace reflected on more than four years of war in Iraq, acknowledging that U.S. planners underestimated the challenges that followed the fall of Saddam Hussein.

“We did not fully understand the depth of the sectarian divisions, and we did not anticipate how quickly the security situation could deteriorate,” Pace said. “Those are mistakes we have to be honest about.”

Pace, a Marine general who became chairman in 2005, has been one of the most visible military leaders during the Iraq conflict. His tenure included the sharp rise in insurgent violence, growing public opposition to the war and the 2007 troop “surge” ordered by President Bush.

Defense Secretary Robert Gates, who replaced Donald Rumsfeld late last year, praised Pace’s service while also acknowledging the Pentagon had faced hard lessons.

“General Pace has served this country with honor, integrity and extraordinary dedication,” Gates said. “At the same time, Iraq has forced all of us — civilian and military leaders alike — to confront assumptions that proved wrong.”

Gates said the military has adapted its strategy in Iraq, including a greater focus on protecting civilians and partnering with Iraqi forces.

“The test now is whether the progress we are seeing can be sustained politically and militarily,” Gates said. “There are no easy answers, and there is no room for complacency.”

Pace said he remains hopeful that the current strategy can improve conditions on the ground, but he cautioned that military success alone cannot solve Iraq’s political divisions.

“Our troops can create security and opportunity,” Pace said. “But Iraq’s leaders must make the decisions necessary for reconciliation. That cannot be done for them.”

Pace’s departure comes after the Bush administration decided not to nominate him for a second term, avoiding what officials said would have been a contentious confirmation fight in the Democratic-controlled Senate. Gates has recommended Adm. Michael Mullen, the chief of naval operations, to succeed him.

Asked how history should judge the Iraq war, Pace said it was too early to know.

“What matters most to me is that the men and women who served there know their mission mattered, and that we as leaders are willing to examine our decisions honestly,” Pace said. “If we fail to learn, then we fail them.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Pace Says Iraq War Needed More Troops, Defends Invasion as Gates Warns Against Failure**

WASHINGTON — Retiring Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Peter Pace said the United States should have deployed more troops in Iraq earlier in the war, even as he continued to defend the 2003 invasion and the decision to remove Saddam Hussein from power.

In farewell remarks marking the end of his four-year tenure as the nation’s top military officer, Pace acknowledged that the U.S. military and civilian leadership underestimated the force required to stabilize Iraq after the fall of Baghdad. He said a larger American presence in the early stages might have helped contain the insurgency and sectarian violence that later engulfed the country.

Still, Pace rejected the argument that the war itself was a mistake, saying Saddam’s regime posed a threat and that U.S. forces had acted honorably under difficult conditions. He praised American troops for their sacrifice and said the mission in Iraq remained central to U.S. security interests.

Defense Secretary Robert Gates, speaking at the same ceremony, warned that a U.S. failure in Iraq would have consequences far beyond Baghdad. He said a collapse of the American effort would embolden extremist movements and give jihadist groups a powerful propaganda victory.

Gates argued that abandoning Iraq before it could achieve a measure of stability would strengthen terrorist networks, destabilize the region and damage U.S. credibility with allies and adversaries alike. His remarks reflected the Bush administration’s position that the war, despite its heavy costs and declining public support, remained a crucial front in the broader fight against terrorism.

Pace’s retirement comes as the United States continues to debate the future of its military presence in Iraq, following the troop “surge” ordered earlier in 2007. While commanders have reported some security gains, the war remains deeply divisive in Washington, with critics calling for a withdrawal timetable and administration officials warning that a rapid pullout could produce chaos.

Pace, a Marine general and Vietnam veteran, is being succeeded by Adm. Mike Mullen as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

counterfactuals.output:
**Bush Accepts Petraeus Recommendations, Signaling Gradual Shift in U.S. Iraq Strategy**

**WASHINGTON —** President George W. Bush has accepted the recommendations of Gen. David H. Petraeus to begin a limited drawdown of U.S. forces in Iraq, marking a cautious turning point in the administration’s war strategy while leaving the central mission — stabilizing Iraq and preventing a wider sectarian collapse — largely intact.

The decision follows Petraeus’ closely watched assessment of the troop “surge,” the additional deployment of U.S. combat brigades ordered earlier this year in an effort to stem spiraling violence, secure Baghdad and Anbar province, and create political space for Iraq’s fragile government. Under the plan endorsed by Bush, some U.S. troops will begin returning home, but the reductions will be gradual and conditions-based, rather than a broad withdrawal sought by many Democrats in Congress.

Administration officials say the drawdown will begin with units already scheduled to leave Iraq, with force levels expected to fall from the surge peak over the coming months. But the White House is making clear that any deeper reductions will depend on battlefield conditions and the ability of Iraqi security forces to assume more responsibility.

Defense Secretary Robert Gates, speaking about the way ahead, described the shift as a measured adjustment rather than a decisive end to the U.S. combat role. Gates has emphasized that commanders must preserve recent security gains while avoiding a sudden reduction that could allow insurgent groups, al-Qaida in Iraq, or Shiite militias to reassert control in contested areas.

Gates said the United States must “look beyond the surge” and move toward a more sustainable posture, but he cautioned that any drawdown must be tied to conditions on the ground. His remarks reflected the Pentagon’s effort to balance military strain — including repeated deployments and pressure on the Army and Marine Corps — against the risk that Iraq could slide back into large-scale sectarian bloodshed.

Gen. Peter Pace, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, also warned that the security improvements remain fragile. Pace has said that U.S. forces have made progress in reducing attacks in some areas, but that Iraq’s political reconciliation has lagged behind military gains. He has stressed that the ultimate outcome depends not only on American combat power, but on the willingness of Iraqi leaders to resolve disputes over power-sharing, oil revenues, provincial authority and the reintegration of former insurgents.

The administration’s revised strategy comes after one of the most violent periods of the Iraq war, triggered in large part by the February 2006 bombing of the Golden Mosque in Samarra, one of Shiite Islam’s holiest shrines. The attack, widely blamed on Sunni extremists linked to al-Qaida in Iraq, unleashed a wave of retaliatory killings, death-squad activity and sectarian cleansing. Baghdad neighborhoods were carved into Sunni and Shiite enclaves, and mixed communities became battlegrounds.

The surge was designed to reverse that trajectory. Petraeus and U.S. Ambassador Ryan Crocker have argued that additional American forces, paired with a new counterinsurgency approach, helped reduce sectarian killings and improve security in parts of Baghdad. U.S. commanders also point to the emergence of Sunni tribal cooperation against al-Qaida in Iraq, particularly in Anbar province, as a major factor in the decline in violence.

But the political picture remains uncertain. While security gains have given the Iraqi government more room to maneuver, Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki’s Shiite-led government has struggled to meet key benchmarks set by Washington. Legislation on de-Baathification reform, oil distribution and provincial elections has moved slowly, raising concerns that military progress may not translate into a durable political settlement.

Democrats criticized Bush’s decision as too limited, arguing that it leaves the United States locked into an open-ended military commitment. Many lawmakers contend that only a firm withdrawal timetable will pressure Iraqi leaders to compromise. Republicans supportive of the president counter that a rapid pullout could squander hard-won gains and empower Iran, al-Qaida and sectarian militias.

The strategy also reflects mounting concern within the Pentagon over the stress placed on the U.S. military. Gates has repeatedly acknowledged that the current pace of deployments is difficult to sustain indefinitely. Senior officers have warned that the Army’s readiness for other contingencies has been strained by years of repeated combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan.

For Bush, accepting Petraeus’ recommendations allows the White House to argue that the surge is producing results while resisting demands for a major strategic reversal. The president is expected to frame the drawdown as evidence that U.S. policy is adapting to improved conditions, not retreating under political pressure.

Still, the central question remains whether reduced violence can be maintained as American troop levels fall. U.S. commanders say Iraqi forces have improved but remain uneven, with some units capable and others plagued by sectarian loyalties, poor logistics and weak leadership. Militias tied to Shiite political factions continue to wield influence, and Sunni insurgent networks remain capable of high-profile bombings.

The aftermath of the Golden Mosque bombing continues to shape American assessments of the war. The explosion did not merely destroy a shrine; it accelerated Iraq’s descent into sectarian war and exposed the weakness of national institutions. U.S. officials now say preventing a return to that cycle is the core objective of the next phase.

As the administration moves forward, Bush’s Iraq policy will rest on a narrow calculation: that U.S. forces can draw down slowly enough to preserve security gains, while Iraqi leaders use the opportunity to build a political order capable of surviving without a large American combat presence. Whether that calculation holds will determine not only the future of Iraq, but the legacy of the war itself.
